chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Where Black bands stayed: rooming houses, and the Lafayette creole woman's house
summary: Hotels were infested so bands used rooming houses; in Lafayette, Louisiana, a woman took him in but her white lover threw his bags onto the porch.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What kind of living -- did you always stay in rooming houses?
There were no hotels. No colored hotels?

Well, the hotels -- well, there were some hotels but the hotels were so crummy, you would have fair better if you lived with a family. You know, if you lived with a family or rooming house, you know. Those hotels were---
Yeah, the hotels had bed bugs and you know, it was just terrible, you know. So if you could find a nice rooming house or some family even that would take you in, you know.

Yeah, speaking of that, we played a town in Lafayette, Louisiana. Now, Lafayette is south of New Orleans, Opelousas. it's near another little town, Apalusa. It's all around there. And most of the Negroes and white there speak Patois French, you know. So everybody got a room when they got -- before we got there but me, and I was standing out here with my bags and every where and I can't find a rooming house. There's no hotel in the town, and I can't find any place to stay. And everybody is kind of squared away.
So here comes a very attractive creole woman by, and I asked her, Miss, do you have an idea of where I can find a room. We're appearing here tonight and we're going to leave tomorrow.

So she said, well, I have a place, you can come and stay at my place. Fine, so I picked my bags up and followed her to her house, and we went in and it was beautiful inside. The sunken bath tub, the hard wood floors, and all that, you know. Geez, I could hardly believe it.

So fine. I put my bags in the room, beautiful room, and I saw -- I had seen a little bar before I, you know, before I saw her and I was going back to the bar to get a drink. So I went to the bar and a lot of the guys were there, and talking and I was telling them about the fabulous place I was staying in and so on and so on. So after having a few drinks I went back, and when I got there my things were out of the room out on the porch. And I went in and there was a white guy, an old white guy there who would not allow me to stay there. This was his mistress. He -- they put me out.
So you see, these are the reasons I -- you know, that I was so glad to get out of the south. I said Mississippi, but the south period.
Was it a promoter, for instance, would never make any kind of arrangements for living accommodations for a band?
No, they didn't care, no, they didn't -- no --
You were on your own, yeah. But
